# Recommended Next.js architecture for a new production application

## Executive recommendation

Start with the **App Router**, a **server-first component tree**, explicit cache/freshness policies, and a **server-only data-access layer (DAL)**. Treat Next.js as the web application and thin backend-for-frontend (BFF) layer—not automatically as the home for every backend workload.

A practical baseline:

```text
src/
  app/
    (marketing)/...
    (product)/...
    (app)/...
    api/.../route.ts            # public HTTP endpoints / webhooks only
    layout.tsx
    error.tsx
    global-error.tsx
  features/<feature>/           # domain UI, schemas, use cases
  lib/dal/                      # server-only queries, authz, DTO mapping
  lib/services/                 # third-party integrations, server-only
  components/                   # genuinely reusable UI
  instrumentation.ts
```

Use route groups for architectural sections and layouts, and colocate route-specific components, loaders, and tests near the routes that consume them. This is a convention for clarity, not a mandated folder taxonomy. Next.js makes only segments with `page` or `route` public. [Project structure](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/project-structure)

## Rendering and UI boundaries

- **Server Components by default.** Fetch/compose data and render non-interactive UI on the server; this keeps secrets out of browser code and avoids unnecessary client JavaScript. [Fetching data](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data)
- **Client Components at interactive leaves only.** Use them for state, effects, browser APIs, rich widgets, or client-only libraries. Keep `"use client"` out of root layouts and broad feature roots unless truly necessary; the production checklist specifically warns that boundary placement can increase browser bundles. [Production checklist](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/production-checklist)
- **Stream intentionally.** Put `Suspense` boundaries—or route-level `loading.tsx` where a whole segment may wait—around slow/uncached portions. Keep shared layouts fast and avoid request-time access there unless the entire layout genuinely must be dynamic. [Fetching data](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data)
- Provide `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx`, and a global error fallback as part of the initial production baseline. [Production checklist](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/production-checklist)

## Data, mutations, and caching

1. **Read directly in Server Components through the DAL.** Do not make a Server Component call your own Route Handler merely to reach the database; that creates an unnecessary server-to-server request. [Production checklist](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/production-checklist)
2. **Use Server Actions for UI-initiated mutations** such as forms. They are not a general read API and should be treated as reachable untrusted POST endpoints.
3. **Use Route Handlers for public HTTP contracts**: browser APIs needed by client code, webhooks, integrations, file-like responses, or a deliberately thin BFF/proxy. Next.js documents this BFF capability but explicitly says it is not a full backend replacement. [Backend for Frontend](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/backend-for-frontend)
4. **Make every cache policy domain-specific.** Decide per read whether the user can receive cached data, for how long, and what mutation/event invalidates it. Current guidance supports `use cache`/`cacheLife`/`cacheTag` and on-demand tag invalidation; the lower-level `fetch` API also exposes explicit cache, revalidation, and tag controls. Prefer tag-based invalidation over broad path invalidation when possible. [Revalidating](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating) · [fetch API](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch)
5. For mutations whose caller must immediately see its own change, use the immediate-expiry semantics (`updateTag`); use stale-while-revalidate tag invalidation where a short delay is acceptable. [Revalidating](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating)

## Security boundary

Create a server-only DAL as the sole place for database access, secret-dependent integrations, authorization checks, and mapping records into minimal DTOs. Re-check authentication, authorization, and input validation inside **each** Server Action and Route Handler—page/layout gating and proxy checks are not sufficient security boundaries. [Data security](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/data-security)

Keep secrets unprefixed; `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables are inlined into the browser bundle at build time. Do not commit `.env*` secrets. [Environment variables](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/environment-variables)

Add a CSP appropriate to the threat model. A nonce-based CSP is not free: it requires dynamic rendering, disables static optimization/ISR, and conflicts with PPR. Use it when that security posture is required; otherwise assess a static header policy. [Content Security Policy](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy)

## Deployment and operations

- Select hosting on capabilities: preserve end-to-end streaming; ensure image support and operational limits fit the app.
- For horizontal/multi-instance deployments, provide shared cache storage and tag-invalidation coordination. Without it, instances can serve divergent cached data after invalidation.
- Add OpenTelemetry instrumentation from the start via `instrumentation.ts`, and send traces/logs/metrics to the team’s chosen backend. [Deploying to platforms](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/deploying-to-platforms) · [OpenTelemetry](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/open-telemetry)
- In CI, run production builds and review the route output for unintentional dynamic behavior; also run production-like performance and security checks before release. [Production checklist](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/production-checklist)

## Decisions that remain application-specific

There is no universal cache duration, data-store choice, authentication provider, monorepo layout, or need for a separate backend service. Choose these from workload requirements: data consistency/freshness, long-running or asynchronous work, real-time connections, integration boundaries, team ownership, compliance, and expected deployment topology.

The core architecture above is verified from official Next.js guidance. One planned version-specific research branch (detailed runtime-selection rules) could not be persisted after the source-budget limit, so this report intentionally avoids making an additional version-specific runtime claim beyond the documented deployment capability requirements.

recentEvidence.fact: The fetch API remains an explicit per-request alternative: `force-cache` enables persistent caching, `no-store` fetches each request, `next.revalidate` defines lifetime, and tags allow revalidateTag invalidation. Request memoization is separate from persistent caching.

Production guidance says to use layouts for shared UI and partial rendering, provide error/404 handling, keep `use client` boundaries narrow, and make request-time API use intentional because it opts routes into dynamic rendering.

Next.js supports a Backend-for-Frontend pattern using publicly reachable Route Handlers, but says its backend capabilities are not a full backend replacement. Server Actions are primarily for frontend mutations and are queued, so they should not be used for data fetching.

For new projects, Next.js recommends a server-only Data Access Layer that controls data access, performs authorization, and returns safe minimal DTOs; application checks must be repeated inside Server Actions and not rely on page-level gating.
Non-public environment variables remain server-only; variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are inlined into browser JavaScript at build time. Env files should not normally be committed.

A Node.js server can run all Next.js features, while streaming is needed to preserve progressive delivery. Multi-instance systems benefit from shared cache and tag coordination; without them, instances independently cache and revalidation does not propagate.
Next.js recommends OpenTelemetry for platform-agnostic observability and supports it out of the box; instrumentation is configured in root/src instrumentation.ts.

CSP helps guard against XSS, clickjacking, and code injection, but nonce-based CSP requires dynamic rendering and disables static optimization/ISR and is incompatible with PPR; direct configured CSP is an option when nonces are unnecessary.

recentFindings.statement: Default to the App Router and model routes with layouts/pages plus loading and error conventions; organize by feature/route using route groups and colocation rather than treating a folder scheme as a framework requirement.
Fetch and compose data on the server by default, stream slow or uncached portions behind localized Suspense/loading boundaries, and add Client Components only at interactive leaves.

Make caching deliberate: use Cache Components (`use cache`, cacheLife, cacheTag) when adopted by the selected Next.js release, or explicit fetch cache/revalidate/tags; favor tag-based invalidation and use updateTag for read-your-own-writes.

Use Server Components to call the DAL directly; use Server Actions for UI-driven mutations, and Route Handlers for public HTTP APIs, browser-accessed endpoints, webhooks, or proxy/BFF needs—not as an internal hop from Server Components.
Centralize database/secrets/authorization in a server-only DAL returning minimal DTOs, and authenticate, authorize, validate, and rate-limit every mutating action or public handler independently.

Choose hosting based on required capabilities, not branding: ensure end-to-end streaming; for multi-instance deployments provision shared cache/tag coordination and stable deployment/action-key configuration; add OpenTelemetry instrumentation from day one.
Adopt CSP and secret hygiene, but evaluate nonce CSP against its all-dynamic rendering and PPR/ISR trade-off.

claimSummaries.statement: For a new production Next.js application, use the App Router with file-based layouts/pages and loading/error conventions; organize by route/feature using colocation and route groups as useful rather than adopting a mandatory folder taxonomy.
Default to server-side data composition in Server Components, isolate slow or uncached work behind localized Suspense/loading boundaries, and keep Client Component boundaries narrow and interactive.

Define explicit cache freshness and invalidation semantics: cache eligible reads, use time or tag-based revalidation, prefer tags over paths where practical, and use immediate tag expiration for read-your-own-writes.

Use a server-only DAL for database/secrets/authorization; call it directly from Server Components, use Server Actions for UI mutations, and use Route Handlers for public HTTP/BFF endpoints rather than an internal Server Component hop.

Production hosting must preserve streaming, and a multi-instance topology needs shared caching/tag coordination for coherent invalidation; add OpenTelemetry instrumentation and apply environment-variable and CSP security controls.
Nonce-based CSP is not a universal default because it makes rendering dynamic and disables static optimization/ISR and PPR; choose it only when its security requirement outweighs those trade-offs.

# OpenCut official automation interfaces

## Bottom line
OpenCut **does not currently document a supported public automation interface**. The official project materials describe these as forthcoming in its rewrite:

- public Editor API;
- third-party plugin system/API;
- MCP server for AI agents;
- headless mode for automation, batch rendering, and CI;
- scripting tab in the editor.

The official README explicitly labels them “What’s coming,” says that `opencut.app` still runs the classic editor, and directs users to the classic version for present-day use. [Official README](https://github.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut)

## What can be used now
There is no documented official endpoint, SDK, CLI, MCP configuration, plugin host, or scripting contract intended for external automation. The documented commands (`moon run web:dev`, `moon run api:dev`, and `moon run desktop:dev`) are developer commands for running the in-progress rewrite—not an automation product interface. [Official README](https://github.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut)

## Status and implications
The official rewrite tracker lists the Editor API design, Plugin API design/host, headless mode, MCP server, and scripting as unfinished work. It says these depend on separating the engine from the UI, and gives no delivery timeline. Therefore, do not design a production integration around any of these planned surfaces yet. [Official rewrite tracker](https://github.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut/issues/811)

## Avoid a common false positive
An MCP/WebSocket implementation was proposed in repository PR #752, with nine timeline-oriented tools, but the PR is **closed** rather than merged. It is not an official currently supported automation interface. [Closed MCP PR #752](https://github.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut/pull/752)

## Practical conclusion
For an integration decision today, treat OpenCut as a user-facing editor rather than an officially automatable editing platform. Any Playwright, fork-based, patched-editor, or community MCP approach would be an unsupported workaround—not an official OpenCut interface.

# OpenCut on macOS: official desktop-app availability

**Answer: no—not as a usable official desktop video editor on 14 September 2026.**

OpenCut’s official repository describes the native desktop target as **“Very early”** and **“just a window that opens.”** Its latest official release notes likewise say the new GPUI/Rust desktop app has a working build setup but **“no features yet.”** The latest release (v0.3.0, published 15 April 2026) has no release assets, so there is no official `.dmg` or other packaged macOS installer to download. [Official desktop README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut/main/apps/desktop/README.md) · [v0.3.0 release record](https://api.github.com/repos/OpenCut-app/OpenCut/releases/latest)

## What can be installed

Only a **developer prototype from source** is officially documented for macOS: install the project’s `proto` tooling, run `proto use`, then `moon run desktop:dev`. This is a build/run workflow, not an end-user installation route. OpenCut’s own main README instead says the previous/classic version is the one “to reach for today,” and that `opencut.app` runs that classic version. [Official repository README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut/main/README.md)

## Important limitation

Even prototype setup may be rough. The official desktop README lists Xcode Command Line Tools, but a July 2026 Apple-Silicon issue report says that was insufficient on the reporter’s setup; full Xcode and the Metal Toolchain were required before the prototype window opened. This is a configuration-specific community report, not a maintainer-confirmed support requirement. [Issue #839](https://github.com/OpenCut-app/OpenCut/issues/839)

## Practical recommendation

Do not install the native OpenCut desktop target if your goal is to edit video in a usable macOS app. Use OpenCut’s official classic web version instead, or wait for an official packaged desktop release with actual editor features. Avoid third-party apps claiming to be “OpenCut desktop,” since they are not the official project’s distribution.
